briefing:
Day 22 ends with the Istanbul Framework Agreement initialed by all parties. This is not yet a signed treaty — the document must return to capitals for formal approval — but it represents the most comprehensive European security settlement since the Helsinki Final Act.

The agreement's key pillars: (1) Nuclear accountability — all 12 warheads accounted for, 90-day IAEA-supervised disposition, Belarus denuclearized; (2) ESAF Framework Agreement — legally binding verification with 12-month review conference; (3) Kaliningrad 40% drawdown over 90 days, OSCE-verified; (4) Phased sanctions relief in three 30-day tranches tied to compliance milestones; (5) EUR 15B reconstruction fund with democratic governance benchmarks; (6) Permanent Istanbul Dialogue Mechanism for ongoing crisis management.

Three things must happen for this to hold: (1) IAEA final certification report (expected Day 23-24 after Smolensk data analysis), (2) formal signatures from all parties (target Day 25-26), and (3) first compliance milestones (Day 30 warhead transport begins, Day 52 first Kaliningrad drawdown verification). The 72-hour verification sprint timeline is on track — Day 24 is the US-Russia joint certification deadline.

Markets exploded upward on the news. Oil dropped to $74, approaching the pre-crisis $73 baseline. The ruble hit 115/USD — strongest since January. European stocks posted their best day since the pandemic recovery.

But the celebration is premature for some. Poland's Sikorski pointedly noted that the Framework Agreement 'is words on paper until the last Russian soldier leaves Kaliningrad on schedule.' And in Moscow, hardliners in the FSB and military establishment are privately furious at what they see as capitulation dressed in diplomatic language. The next 90 days will test whether words become reality.

Day 23 agenda: IAEA final report preparation, Constitutional Court hearing on Orban in Budapest, formal signature preparation, first compliance planning meetings.
narrative:
Day 22 delivers the moment the world has been waiting for: the IAEA confirms both missing nuclear warheads are present and intact at Russia's Smolensk Oblast storage facility, and the Istanbul II Summit produces the framework for a comprehensive settlement. The crisis that began with Russian tanks rolling through the Suwalki Gap ends — in principle — with signatures on the Bosphorus.

The day begins at 06:00 when the IAEA three-person verification team, led by senior inspector Markus Brenner, arrives at the Smolensk-14 military storage complex. Russian military personnel provide full access — bunker doors opened, serial numbers checked, radiation signatures verified against the Asipovichy baseline data. By 10:47, Director General Grossi issues a preliminary statement from Vienna: 'Both warheads identified by serial number match the missing Asipovichy inventory. Physical condition is consistent with controlled storage. IAEA can confirm that all twelve Russian tactical nuclear warheads deployed to Belarus are now accounted for.' The news reaches the Istanbul Format session mid-morning, and the negotiating dynamic shifts instantly. The nuclear accountability precondition that had dominated every discussion for a week is satisfied.

The Istanbul Format morning session (09:00-13:30) produces the Istanbul Framework Agreement — a 47-page document hammered out by exhausted diplomats. The three gaps close: warhead disposition within 90 days under IAEA custody and monitoring; the European Security Architecture Framework (ESAF) adopted as a Framework Agreement with legally binding verification protocols and a 12-month review conference; phased sanctions relief beginning 30 days after IAEA certification of nuclear compliance, structured in three tranches tied to Kaliningrad drawdown milestones. Russia's Lavrov accepts the 90-day warhead timeline after an 11:00 private conversation with Trump's envoy Witkoff — the final push. Lavrov tells the room: 'Russia chooses the path of transparency.'

The all-nations plenary at 14:00 is historic. Erdogan opens with a keynote celebrating Turkey's mediation. Trump and Putin deliver brief joint remarks — carefully choreographed to avoid the appearance of either side winning. Sikorski delivers the frontline address: fifteen minutes of controlled fury, listing the Lithuanian villages shelled, the Polish pilot captured, the families displaced — then pivoting to Poland's red lines woven into the Framework Agreement: permanent enhanced NATO presence confirmed, no force caps, ICC accountability preserved. The Belarus transitional council chairman Sakhashchyk receives a standing ovation when he addresses the plenary — the first time a post-Lukashenko Belarus has been recognized on the world stage. Hungary's delegation, led by President Sulyok's representative (not Orban), quietly signs onto the Framework Agreement without objection.

surprises: At 16:45, during a coffee break after the plenary statements, Russian Defense Minister Belousov is observed making an urgent phone call in the Ciragan Palace garden. Turkish intelligence, monitoring the grounds, intercepts fragments: Belousov is speaking to someone at the General Staff in Moscow, saying 'Gerasimov must understand — the Framework is the framework. There will be no renegotiation. Anyone who obstructs implementation answers to the President personally.' The intercept suggests that while Putin has accepted the deal, elements of the Russian military establishment are already pushing back against the 90-day timelines. Turkey shares this with the US delegation, confirming the intelligence about restive Russian generals — the Dubai meetings were not about post-Putin planning, but about hedging against exactly this kind of internal resistance to a settlement Putin's hardliners view as surrender.

At 21:30 Istanbul time, Peter Magyar — the Hungarian opposition leader who has been demanding snap elections — arrives at Istanbul's Ataturk Airport on a commercial flight from Budapest. He has not been invited to the summit, but he holds an impromptu press conference at the airport arrivals hall, declaring: 'Tomorrow the Constitutional Court will end the Orban era. I have come to Istanbul to tell the world that the new Hungary will be a loyal European partner.' Hungarian media broadcast it live. In Budapest, sources report that Orban has not left Felcsut in 72 hours and is refusing to take calls from his own party's parliamentary leadership. The premiership is functionally vacant.
